newsitem.title: IRAN: FEATURE - Iran's revolutionary leader leaves uncertain legacy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Iran's revolutionary leader leaves uncertain legacy.

text.p: Four minarets and a dull gold dome poke out of a nest of scaffolding shimmering in the smog that hangs over south Tehran, a shrine to the grim-faced leader of Iran's Islamic revolution, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.
A noisy motorway leading south to the holy city of Qom runs past the unfinished mosque.
Several hundred faithful gather for prayers inside but fail to fill its vast interior, which, with its metal roof supports and the cold light, resembles an aircraft hangar.
Khomeini, whose stern gaze graces countless hoardings across Tehran, is Iran's equivalent to Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin in the country's revolutionary pantheon.
"Dear Khomeini -- we will never pull down the flag you have raised," runs one typical slogan in the crowded city.
But Khomeini's tomb has none of the gloomy formality surrounding the Soviet leader's waxen form on Moscow's Red Square.
An elderly mullah in a loose white turban kneels, squints through a magnifying glass at a battered copy of the Koran and mumbles the verses.

He ignores wide-eyed boys and girls, their faces framed in white scarves. They giggle as they chase each other in a game of tag, while their indulgent mothers bite into snow-white bricks of nougat as they watched.
To one side of the mosque, a cage of aluminium and scratched perspex covers Khomeini's simple tomb, a rectangular block of marble covered in felt of Islamic green.
Men, some in tears, queue to pay their respects and stuff rial notes through cracks in the perspex where they flutter down to join a large pile of cash, like coins in a fountain.
Across a rope barrier, and watched by a couple of bored Revolutionary Guards, women in black chador robes squat on tattered carpets on the cold marble floor.
KHOMEINI STILL RESPECTED

Mohammed Sadegh Kermanshahi, on a visit to the tomb, wears the tawny gown of a Moslem cleric. He remembers seeing Khomeini during the violent 1979 revolution which overthrew the Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
"When we saw the Imam we cried because he was such an important man of Islam," says the 33-year-old. "He was not afraid of America or the Shah. He was only afraid of God."

While the wealthy sophisticates of north Tehran may chafe at the strict Islamic dress codes and sip powerful Armenian-made moonshine in front of illegal satellite television, Khomeini remains a potent, respected figure for the majority of Iranians.
"People have a deep affection for what he did in the revolution," said Ibrahim Yazdi, whose opposition Freedom Movement is one of the few tolerated by the Iranian authorities.
Yazdi, a former Iranian foreign minister, accompanied Khomeini on his dramatic return from exile in France to Iran in 1979.
"They're loyal to the revolution and Mr Khomeini played a vital role, his charisma was very deep," said Yazdi.
IRAN AT IDEOLOGICAL CROSSROADS
But presidential elections are due in May and the Islamic republic is at an ideological crossroads between hardliners and moderates.
"This chapter of our history and the revolution has not been concluded yet," Yazdi warned.
Following Khomeini's death in 1989, Iran -- much like the Soviet Union after Lenin died -- lacks an unquestioned political arbiter and is now prey to similar smoky, backstairs intrigue.
"There isn't much ideological Islam any more," said a Western diplomat in Tehran. "It's really a series of competing, anarchic factions."
Iran's parliamentary speaker, Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, is widely seen as the front-runner in the managed presidential race. He stands for the reinforcement of Islamic law favoured by the hardliners.
But political rivalries within the hazy confines permitted by the republic's Islamic guardians appear to leave many Iranians cold.
PRICES, NOT ISLAM, MAIN CONCERN
Discontent centres on low salaries, rising prices and a flourishing black market -- not on around the amount of hair women can get away with revealing under their chadors.
"People are fed up with the mullahs for their corruption," the diplomat said.
Built on one side of Khomeini's shrine is a branch of the state-owned Refah department store, crowded with shoppers hoping to pick up a bargain among the subsidised goods.
Women crowd over a counter selling fluorescent green and lemon hairbands -- a splash of colour against their drab, uniform of revolutionary black.
Asked if life had improved since the revolution, one man, shopping with his family and nervous of being overheard, ventured only: "Things are very expensive now."
